subject: English Language

source.title: Primary School Education Curriculum Design — English Language, Grade 5 (First Published 2017, Revised 2024)
source.notes: Read directly from 'grade 5 designs/GRADE-5-ENGLISH-LANGUAGE-Curriculum-Designs.pdf' via the Read tool (no pages param), full text extracted. The design is organised as 13 real-world THEMES (Child Rights and Responsibilities, National Celebrations, Etiquette-Table Manners, Road Accidents - Prevention, Traditional Foods, Jobs and Occupations, Learning Through Technology, The Farm-Cash Crops, Communicable Diseases, Leisure Time Activities, Sports - Appreciating Talents, Environmental Pollution, Money - Savings and Banking), each carrying exactly 4 sub-strands: 1 Listening and Speaking, 1 Reading, 1 Grammar in Use, 1 Writing = 52 sub-strands, 150 lessons. Same shape as the Grade 6/7/8 English builds (see curriculum-reference/grade-6/english.json): STRANDS in curriculum.ts are the 4 columns, NOT the 13 themes; each sub-strand maps to one skill file. SUMMARY OF STRANDS AND SUB-STRANDS table (p.xii) groups the sub-strand types as: Listening and Speaking = Listening comprehension / Pronunciation and vocabulary / Speaking fluency (38 lessons); Reading = Extensive reading / Intensive reading / Fluency (39 lessons); Grammar in Use = Word classes / Language patterns / Tense (36 lessons); Writing = Creative writing / Functional writing / Mechanics of writing (36 lessons). The 'themes' array below captures the theme-level SUGGESTED VOCABULARY plus fixed phrases, similes, idioms, proverbs and phrasal verbs blocks verbatim — these are major content pools feeding every Listening & Speaking and Writing (similes/proverbs) skill for that theme. Grade 5's own 'Lesson Allocation at Upper Primary' table gives English 5 lessons/week.

subjectGeneralLearningOutcomes: Listen for the main idea and specific information from a variety of print and digital texts
Speak, at the right speed, accurately, and with expression on a variety of subjects and genres
Read a variety of texts fluently, interpretively, and with comprehension for lifelong learning
Use grammatical forms to communicate ideas, opinions, and emotions appropriately in different settings
Write texts for various purposes legibly, accurately, creatively, and cohesively for self-expression
Apply Digital Literacy skills to enhance their language competency
assessmentSignal: Appendix 1 rubrics — 'Meets expectation' rows: SPEAKING 'Speaks accurately with expression and at the right speed, with minimum hesitation for fluency'; READING FLUENCY 'Reads about 300 words fluently and accurately at the right speed and with expression' (the 'Exceeds' row says 'more than 350 words'; note the printed 'Approaches' row's '800 words' is a typo for a lower band); READING COMPREHENSION 'Reads the text and relates the ideas to real life experiences'; EXTENSIVE READING 'Selects and reads relevant materials of between 1000-1250 words for information and pleasure'; GRAMMAR 'Uses grammatical forms to communicate ideas, opinions, and emotions appropriately in different settings for effective communication'; WRITING 'Uses punctuation, paragraphing and spelling correctly' + 'Writes a variety of writings using the correct formats' + 'Writes creative works clearly and expressively'.
learningResources: Non-digital: course books, story books, poetry books, pictures and photographs, newspapers, magazines, junior encyclopedia, journals, dictionaries, diorama, flash cards, word wheels, word puzzles, code words, charts and realia
Digital: digital story books, electronic/online dictionaries, electronic and digital devices, flash cards, charts, video clips, audio-visual resources, other web resources

How do we learn to spell words correctly?
learningExperiences: Discuss with peers the words they find difficult to spell
Make a presentation on correct spelling of homophones and homonyms
Write words from a dictation by the teacher or from an audio-visual recording
Play spelling games with peers; for example, scramble or scrabble
Use a jigsaw puzzle to form words correctly with peers
Make words from jumbled up letters
scopeNotes: include: homophone = same sound, different spelling & meaning — their/there/they're, to/too/two, your/you're, its/it's, here/hear, know/no, write/right, one/won, sea/see, week/weak, piece/peace, plain/plane, break/brake, whole/hole, flour/flower, past/passed, threw/through, road/rode

include: homonym = same spelling & sound, different meaning — bat (animal / sports), bark (dog / tree), match (sports / firestick), pitch (field / throw / sound), left (direction / departed), fair (just / event / light), spring (season / coil / water source), well (healthy / water source / adverb)

include: commonly misspelt words — because, friend, beautiful, necessary, separate, February, Wednesday, address, occurred, receive, believe, definitely, environment, government, sincerely, tomorrow, until, which, weird, exercise

subStrands.name: 12.4 Functional Writing: Diary — appointment diary; journal (3 days) (Environmental Pollution)
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify the key components of a diary/journal from a sample diary/journal
Create a journal/diary to convey desired information in the right format
Collaborate with peers to create personal journals and diaries on varied topics
keyInquiryQuestions: Why should we plan our activities in advance?
What is the most memorable experience in your life?
learningExperiences: View a sample diary/journal and identify the components
Write journal/diary entries with peers
Create an appointment diary collaboratively
Create a three-day journal with peers
Display their work in class and take a gallery walk
Give feedback to each group about their work after the gallery walk
Search for examples of diaries or journals on the internet, textbooks or the library
Create a diary or journal individually
scopeNotes: include: appointment diary = dated entries listing planned activities with times (like a timetable of what WILL happen)

include: journal/personal diary = dated first-person entries recording what DID happen and how the writer felt; components — date (and sometimes day/time), entry in first person, past tense for events, feelings/reflection, informal tone

subStrands.name: 13.4 Spelling — homophones; words with double consonants; words with double vowels (Money - Savings and Banking)
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify homophones, words with double consonants and words with double vowels correctly
Spell homophones, words with double consonants and words with double vowels correctly
Use homophones, words with double consonants and words with double vowels in sentences correctly
Recommend to peers ways of enhancing their spelling skills for clarity of communication
Collaborate with others to judge the appropriateness of words, phrases and sentences used in own or provided documents
keyInquiryQuestions: Why should we write words correctly?
Which words have the same pronunciation but different spelling?
learningExperiences: Identify homophones, words with double consonants such as slipped, clapping, carefully and words with double vowels from a text
Listen to words read by the teacher or from audio recording, for example: waist/waste, collect/dropped
Write down words from a dictation correctly
Use a jigsaw puzzle to form words correctly with peers
Make words from jumbled up letters
Form sentences from the words they have spelt
Search for homophones, words with double consonants and words with double vowels from the internet
scopeNotes: include: double consonants — slipped, clapping, carefully, dropped, running, swimming, beginning, hammer, dinner, ladder, arrow, bottle, little, happy, funny, kettle, pillow, lesson, address, borrow, mirror, rabbit, button, cannot, common, cottage, jelly, penny, sudden, summer, tunnel, village, yellow

include: double vowels — book, look, cook, foot, moon, soon, food, root, tooth, spoon, wood, good, feet, meet, seen, tree, three, green, sleep, deep, keep, week, need, seed, feel, wheel, teeth, cheese, coffee, agree, balloon

include: homophones — waist/waste, collect (no homophone; paired for dictation with dropped), see/sea, be/bee, blue/blew, cent/scent/sent, cell/sell, allowed/aloud, board/bored, buy/by/bye, coarse/course, sole/soul, sum/some, tail/tale, wait/weight, wear/where, won/one
